learningObjectives: Explain how Personas, Access Roles, and Access Groups control user access in Pega applications.
Describe how ARO and Access Deny records manage Case Type permissions and how production levels affect access control.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Personas, Access Roles, and Access Groups

elements.text: Think of an Access Group as a configured set of hotel permissions, with Access Roles contributing the rules for rooms and actions. A Persona describes a user group’s goals; it is not itself a universal permission grant. Evaluate the applicable restrictions as well as grants.

elements.description: Defines how users align with an application by BUSINESS OUTCOMES. Example: 'Loan Applicant' and 'Loan Officer' have different goals in the process. Creating a Persona in App Studio auto-creates a corresponding Access Group in Dev Studio.
Defines how users INTERACT with the application. Example: Manager, User. Each Role has a default Channel interface — this determines which screen users see upon login.

Categorizes users by job function. For each Access Role, you configure permissions to control Actions on instances of a specific class. Example: 'Manager' and 'User' can be separate Access Roles with different permissions.

Represents a group of privileges. Each Access Group references one or more Access Roles. Multiple Access Groups can reference the same application for different access levels and align with roles assignable to users in App Studio.

In the lesson’s ordinary conflicting-role example, the most permissive setting applies. Do not extend this example into a promise that other security checks, Access Deny conditions or authorization models are bypassed.

elements.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 190" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>User goals and configured access</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="var(--pa-brand)">User goals and configured access</text><g font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)"><text x="30" y="78">Persona: user goals; Access Group: application and Access Roles.</text><text x="30" y="110">Access Role → class permission records (ARO / Access Deny).</text><text x="30" y="142">A Persona and an Access Group are related, not identical.</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Persona and Access Group relationship; Access Roles contain class permission rules.

elements.term: ARO — Access of Role to Object
elements.description: Access of Role to Object binds an Access Role to permissions for a class. Permissions can allow actions or specify No Access; the record is not limited to unconditional grants.

Access Deny supplies explicit denial over the applicable ARO permission. Evaluate its conditions and production-level settings; do not assume every role’s grant and every denial combine identically in all configurations.

elements.term: Best practice: use management tools, not direct record edits
elements.description: Prefer App Studio User management when sufficient. Some permissions, including Case deletion, require Access Manager. Both simplify the underlying role permissions:
items: App Studio: Users → User management (Persona access landing page)
Dev Studio: Configure → Org & Security → Access Manager
bulletPoints: Use Rule forms when production-level values other than the tools’ 0/5 settings are needed; direct Rule configuration is not categorically forbidden.

elements.description: On-premises levels: 5 Production, 4 Staging, 3 Quality assurance, 2 Development, 1 Sandbox. Access value 0 denies; otherwise the permission value must be at least the system production level. A value of 2 can permit Development while denying Production.

elements.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 760 190" role="img" font-family="inherit"><title>Production level and permission values</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="170" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><text x="30" y="42" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="var(--pa-brand)">Production level and permission values</text><g font-size="14" fill="var(--pa-ink-2)"><text x="30" y="78">5 Production • 4 Staging • 3 QA • 2 Development • 1 Sandbox.</text><text x="30" y="110">0 denies; nonzero permission value must be ≥ system level.</text><text x="30" y="142">Tools set 0/5; Rule forms allow intermediate values.</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Correct production scale and permission comparison; direct Rule forms support intermediate levels.

examPitfalls.title: Persona ≠ Role — different purposes
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Do not confuse a business Persona with the underlying permission records or assume that a Persona is mandatory for every Access Group.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Persona = business outcomes alignment. Role = interaction pattern with the app. Each Role has a default Channel interface that determines the login screen.

examPitfalls.title: Conflicting permissions → MOST PERMISSIVE wins
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The basic conflict example chooses the permissive setting; it does not eliminate applicable explicit denial or other authorization checks.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Apply the example within its assumptions, and inspect the full authorization configuration.

examPitfalls.title: ARO permissions and applicable Access Deny
examPitfalls.trapDescription: ARO can specify No Access. Access Deny adds explicit denial; it is not a reason to skip evaluating configuration conditions.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: ARO defines class permissions; Access Deny overrides applicable ARO access. Evaluate production levels and conditions.

examPitfalls.title: Management tools first; Rule forms for intermediate levels
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Treating direct edits as always forbidden prevents configuring values other than 0 or 5.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Prefer management tools where sufficient; use underlying Rule forms for intermediate production-level values.

examPitfalls.title: Production scale: 5 Production, 1 Sandbox
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Reversing the scale also reverses how numeric permission values are interpreted.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: 5 Production; 4 Staging; 3 QA; 2 Development; 1 Sandbox. Nonzero permission value ≥ system level grants the action.

examPitfalls.title: Persona → Access Group: not all Access Groups have a Persona
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask whether every Access Group must have a corresponding Persona. Candidates say yes. A Persona maps to an Access Group, but an Access Group can exist without any Persona — system-level groups (admins, developers) typically have no Persona.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Creating a Persona in App Studio auto-creates a corresponding Access Group in Dev Studio. However, not all Access Groups in Dev Studio have a corresponding Persona in App Studio.

examPitfalls.title: Access Manager path in Dev Studio
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Do not insert Authentication into the Access Manager navigation path.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Dev Studio Access Manager: Configure → Org & Security → Access Manager. App Studio: Users → User management (Persona access landing page).

How users interact with the application interface
The permissions assigned to each user role
The default channel interface for each user at login

optionExplanations.A: Persona describes business outcomes and user goals.
optionExplanations.B: Interaction tasks describe the role concept.
optionExplanations.C: Specific permissions are configured through access records.
optionExplanations.D: The Channel is an interface association, not the Persona definition.

optionExplanations.C: List order is not the rule in this example.
optionExplanations.D: The described conflict does not require that error.

optionExplanations.B: Explicit override denial is the Access Deny purpose.
optionExplanations.C: OTP delivery is a different security configuration.
optionExplanations.D: A Channel interface is not a class permission record.

Categorizes users by job function. Permissions control Actions on instances of specific classes.
Access Groups reference role sets. Ordinary conflicting-role example: permissive setting, subject to applicable restrictions.
Access of Role to Object defines class permissions, including No Access. Access Deny adds explicit applicable denial.
Prefer User management or Access Manager; Rule forms support values other than the tools’ 0/5.
5 Production, 4 Staging, 3 QA, 2 Development, 1 Sandbox. Nonzero access value must be ≥ system level.
